notes.title: How the cuisine filters were policed
notes.body: Every food card names a specific dish — a cuisine label alone doesn’t qualify. The Greater Region’s canon crosses three countries: the Saarland Schwenker and Dibbelabbes/Gefillde, Luxembourg’s Judd mat Gaardebounen and Gromperekichelcher, Lorraine quiche & tarte aux mirabelles, and Mosel Riesling from steep-slope Weinstuben — with a deep Michelin bench (Christian Bau 3★ on the DE/FR/LU tripoint). A cuisine tag names the kitchen’s own tradition, never one dish it happens to serve.

notes.title: Web-searched in-language and fact-checked
notes.body: Every place is traceable to a credible source — Michelin, UNESCO, Gault&Millau, the Saarbrücker Zeitung, SR, Le Républicain Lorrain, Inspire Metz, the Luxembourg Times/Luxemburger Wort, Visit Luxembourg, the Trierischer Volksfreund, DW Travel, local university & ESN guides and vetted local creators — recorded in data/sources.json. Every coordinate is verified into data/geocodes.json and every place status-checked open. Yelp/TripAdvisor never count toward the two-source bar.

places.n: Place Stanislas, Place de la Carrière & Place d'Alliance
places.w: Nancy's UNESCO-listed ensemble (since 1983) and one of the most harmonious urban compositions of the Enlightenment: the gilded 18th-century royal square built 1752-1756 for Duke Stanislas Leszczynski by architect Emmanuel Héré, with Jean Lamour's wrought-iron gates and gilded fountains, linked by the tree-lined Place de la Carrière to the smaller Place d'Alliance. The masterpiece of the ducal city.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Place Stanislas)

places.ad: 36-38 Rue du Sergent Blandan, 54000 Nancy, France
places.w: The temple of Nancy Art Nouveau — the only museum in France devoted to the École de Nancy movement led by Émile Gallé, Louis Majorelle, the Daum brothers and Jacques Gruber. Set in a 1900s villa with fully furnished rooms, glass, furniture, ceramics, stained glass and a garden, it makes the case for Nancy as Art Nouveau's second capital after Brussels.

pv.src: Wikipedia coordinate (differs ~0.7km from latitude.to; street/town-level)

places.w: The first wholly Art Nouveau house in Nancy, designed 1901-1902 by Henri Sauvage for cabinetmaker Louis Majorelle — a total artwork uniting Majorelle's ironwork and furniture, Jacques Gruber's stained glass and Alexandre Bigot's stoneware. Labelled a 'Maison des Illustres' and reopened after restoration, it is the only Art Nouveau house in the city open to visitors year-round.

pv.src: Wikidata Q16964856 (Villa Majorelle)

places.n: Palais des Ducs de Lorraine – Musée Lorrain
places.w: The former palace of the Dukes of Lorraine in the Ville-Vieille, its late-15th-century Porterie one of the first Renaissance works in eastern France. The Musée Lorrain inside holds over 150,000 works telling Lorraine's history from prehistory to today, spread across the ducal palace, its garden and the adjoining Cordeliers church and convent.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2081177 / Wikipedia (Palace of the Dukes of Lorraine)

places.w: On Place Stanislas itself, one of France's oldest fine-art museums (founded 1793): European painting from the 14th century to now, a strong Lorraine collection, and a spectacular basement gallery of Daum glass built into the city's medieval fortifications.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Museum of Fine Arts of Nancy)

places.ad: Rue de la Craffe, 54000 Nancy, France
places.w: The twin-towered 14th-century gate that guarded the northern entrance to Nancy's old town until 1610, through which the Dukes of Lorraine made their entry — the most striking surviving remnant of the medieval city walls.

pv.src: FR Wikipedia/Wikidata Q659783 (Porte de la Craffe)

places.w: A neo-Gothic jewel in the heart of the Ville-Vieille, built 1864-1871 by architect Prosper Morey with stained glass from the Carl Geyling workshops and altars donated by kings and emperors. Its soaring spire is a landmark of old Nancy.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Saint-Epvre Basilica)

places.w: Nancy's beloved 23-hectare central park just off Place Stanislas — a former tree nursery laid out in the 18th century, with shaded alleys, a rose garden, a small zoo, a bandstand and a Rodin statue of the painter Claude Lorrain. The city's favourite green space.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3364226 (Parc de la Pépinière)

places.w: A much-loved combination of tropical aquarium and natural-history museum run with the University of Lorraine — reef tanks on the ground floor beneath galleries of zoology and taxidermy upstairs. A family fixture near the Pépinière.

pv.src: Wikipedia infobox (Aquarium Museum, Nancy)

places.w: Nancy's opera house on the corner of Place Stanislas, built by Joseph Hornecker of the École de Nancy and inaugurated in 1919, blending classical composition with Art Nouveau detail. One of France's national opera companies, worth seeing for the building alone.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3354579 (Opéra national de Lorraine)

places.w: Nancy's 18th-century cathedral in the Ville-Neuve, a monumental classical church built 1703-1742 with a grand organ and a rotunda painted by the Nancy artist Claude Jacquart — the seat of the diocese and a quieter counterpoint to the Art Nouveau and baroque sights.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Nancy Cathedral)

places.n: Chambre de Commerce et d'Industrie (Art Nouveau)
places.w: One of the great built statements of the École de Nancy — the 1908 Chamber of Commerce building whose interior gathers stained glass, ironwork and marquetry by Nancy's Art Nouveau masters, including landscapes of Lorraine in glass. A highlight of the city's Art Nouveau trail.

pv.src: Geoportail (CCI, 53 rue Stanislas)

places.w: Nancy's grand covered market in a U-shaped 1852 neoclassical hall between Place Charles III and Rue Saint-Dizier, with a glass-roofed 2017 courtyard added. More than sixty stalls of Lorraine produce — quiche, pâté lorrain, mirabelle, bergamote, the century-old Marchand cheese affineurs — plus counters to eat on the spot.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3289847 (Marché couvert de Nancy)

places.ad: Avenue du Maréchal Juin, 54000 Nancy, France
places.w: A leafy 7.5-hectare public garden southwest of the centre, near the Art Nouveau villas of the Thermal quarter, with a magnolia classed a 'Remarkable Tree of France' and a pavilion from the 1909 international exhibition. A pleasant pairing with a Villa Majorelle walk.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3363904 (Parc Sainte-Marie)

places.ad: Place de la Cathédrale, 67000 Strasbourg, France
places.w: The pink-sandstone Gothic masterpiece at the heart of the Grande Île, its single spire completed in 1439 and the tallest structure in Christendom until the 19th century. Inside, the 19th-century astronomical clock by Schwilgué springs to life daily at 12:30, and the platform gives a sweeping view over the city; entry to the church is free.

pv.src: Wikipedia infobox (Strasbourg Cathedral)

places.w: Strasbourg's historic core — the island bounded by the Ill, inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1988 and extended in 2017 to take in the German-era Neustadt. Together they read as a lesson in European city-building, from the medieval Grande Île to the monumental Haussmann-meets-Germanic avenues of the imperial new town.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Grande Île, Strasbourg)

places.ad: Quai de la Petite France, 67000 Strasbourg, France
places.w: The postcard quarter of the Grande Île — the former tanners' and fishermen's district, a maze of cobbled lanes and half-timbered houses from the 16th and 17th centuries leaning over the canals of the Ill, the most photographed being the galleried Maison des Tanneurs. Part of the UNESCO site.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Petite France, Strasbourg)

places.ad: Quai de la Bruche, 67000 Strasbourg, France
places.w: The medieval Covered Bridges with their three surviving watchtowers and, just upstream, the Barrage Vauban — a pink-sandstone dam-bridge built 1686-1690 to Vauban's plans, its terrace giving the classic panorama over Petite France. Part of the UNESCO Grande Île.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Ponts Couverts, Strasbourg)

places.w: The former prince-bishops' palace beside the cathedral, an 18th-century masterpiece housing three museums under one roof — the Archaeological Museum, the Museum of Decorative Arts (with its sumptuous state apartments) and the Museum of Fine Arts. Strasbourg's grandest cultural address.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Palais Rohan, Strasbourg)

places.w: A folk-life museum of old Alsace spread through a warren of Renaissance timber-framed houses on the Ill — reconstructed interiors, painted furniture, costumes, ceramics and the everyday objects of pre-industrial rural Alsace, reached by creaking galleries and wooden staircases.

pv.src: EN/FR Wikipedia infobox (Musée alsacien)

places.ad: 1 Place Hans Jean Arp, 67000 Strasbourg, France
places.w: Strasbourg's big glass-roofed museum of modern and contemporary art beside the Barrage Vauban, strong on Kandinsky, Arp, Ernst and the Strasbourg-born abstraction of Jean Arp and Sophie Taeuber-Arp, with a rooftop café over Petite France.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Strasbourg Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art)

places.w: The largest square of the city centre and its meeting point, named for the Strasbourg-born general Jean-Baptiste Kléber whose statue stands at the centre, framed by the 18th-century Aubette building. The city's giant Christmas tree stands here in Advent.

pv.src: Wikipedia/Wikidata Q1753950 (Place Kléber)

places.n: Quartier européen – Parlement européen & Palais de l'Europe
places.w: Strasbourg's identity as a European capital made visible: the European Parliament's 1999 hemicycle building, the Council of Europe's Palais de l'Europe (1977), the European Court of Human Rights and ARTE, gathered north of the Orangerie. The Parliament welcomes some 140,000 visitors a year.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Seat of the European Parliament, Louise Weiss building)

places.w: Strasbourg's oldest and grandest park, laid out in the 18th century and remodelled by the landscape gardener of Napoleon III, opposite the European institutions — a lake with rowing boats, a small zoo and stork enclosure (the Alsatian emblem), and the Josephine pavilion. Free and much loved by locals.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3364190 (Parc de l'Orangerie)

places.w: The 'cathedral of Alsatian Protestantism' — a rare five-nave hall church, largely 13th-15th century, holding the monumental Baroque mausoleum of Marshal Maurice de Saxe by Pigalle and a Silbermann organ once played by Albert Schweitzer and Mozart.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1785858 (St Thomas' Church, Strasbourg)

places.ad: Place de la République, 67000 Strasbourg, France
places.w: The monumental heart of the German-built Neustadt, a circular garden square ringed by grand imperial buildings — the Palais du Rhin, the National and University Library, the Théâtre National de Strasbourg and the Préfecture — and a keystone of the UNESCO extension.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Place de la République, Strasbourg)

places.n: Musée Tomi Ungerer – Centre international de l'illustration
places.ad: 2 Avenue de la Marseillaise, 67000 Strasbourg, France
places.w: France's first museum devoted to illustration, in a 19th-century villa near the Contades — 14,000 drawings by the Strasbourg-born artist Tomi Ungerer, from beloved children's books to biting satire and erotica, that he gave to his home city.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Tomi Ungerer Museum)

places.w: A hidden monument of the modern avant-garde: the leisure-complex interiors Theo van Doesburg, Hans Arp and Sophie Taeuber-Arp created in 1928 inside the 18th-century Aubette on Place Kléber — 'the Sistine Chapel of abstraction' — restored and reopened, and free to visit.

pv.src: Wikidata Q758467 (Aubette)

places.ad: Place du Général de Gaulle, 67700 Saverne, France
places.w: The 'little Versailles of Alsace' — the vast 18th-century pink-sandstone palace of the prince-bishops of Strasbourg on the Marne-Rhine canal at Saverne, its 140 m garden facade one of the longest in France. Now a museum of archaeology, art and the writer-activist Louise Weiss. A gateway sight on the Nancy-Strasbourg corridor.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1670612 (Rohan Castle, Saverne)

places.n: Vitrail 'La Paix' de Chagall – Chapelle des Cordeliers, Sarrebourg
places.w: Marc Chagall's monumental stained-glass window 'La Paix' (Peace), 12 m high, glowing in the deconsecrated Chapelle des Cordeliers at Sarrebourg, with the companion 'Paix' tapestry in the town museum — the highlight of a Chagall trail on the corridor between Nancy and Strasbourg.

pv.src: Wikidata Q195052 (Chapelle des Cordeliers, Sarrebourg)

places.n: Obernai – cité médiévale & Place du Marché
places.w: The second-most-visited town of the Bas-Rhin after Strasbourg — a walled Decapolis city at the foot of Mont Sainte-Odile whose market square gathers the 1554 Kornhalle grain hall, the 1523 town hall, the six-bucket Renaissance well and the 60 m Kapellturm belfry. A wine-road gateway rich in half-timbered houses.

pv.src: Wikidata Q15950904 (20 place du Marché, Obernai)

places.w: Alsace's spiritual summit — a 763 m sandstone promontory crowned by the convent founded in the 7th century by St Odile, patron of Alsace, ringed by the mysterious prehistoric 'Mur Païen'. A pilgrimage and viewpoint drawing well over a million visitors a year, 15 minutes above Obernai.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Mont Sainte-Odile)

places.w: Saarbrücken's alternative, creative quarter — a dense grid of quirky pubs, cafés, small shops and street art just east of the old town, engaged in art and music and beloved by students and locals. The city's best evening wandering, and now home to a cluster of MICHELIN-listed kitchens as well as old-school Kneipen.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1972159 / de.wikipedia (Nauwieser Viertel) infobox

places.w: The city's farmers' market on the baroque St. Johanner Markt square — regional producers with fruit, vegetables, sausage, fish, bread and cheese several mornings a week (Mon/Wed/Fri), plus a Saturday Bauernmarkt of regional and organic produce. The place to taste and buy Saarland's larder.

pv.src: Wikidata Q15848504 (St. Johanner Markt) - weekly market held on this square

places.w: The former Mousel brewery on the Alzette below the old town, converted in 2008 into Luxembourg City's liveliest nightlife strip — a row of bars, restaurants and clubs, each with its own style, so you can hop several in one evening. The heart of the capital's young weekend scene.

pv.src: Wikidata Q519726 (Clausen district centroid); the Rives de Clausen complex is in Clausen

places.w: One of Metz's most picturesque squares — a long medieval arcade of some sixty pointed arches raised by Lombard money-changers on the old Roman wall, its houses keeping crenellations and Renaissance balconies. The former 'place du Change' and today a lively, café-lined heart of the old town.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3390099 (Place Saint-Louis, Metz)

places.ad: Place de la Comédie, Île du Petit-Saulcy, 57000 Metz, France
places.w: A striking neo-Romanesque Protestant church of 1901–04, built of grey stone during the German annexation on the little island of Petit-Saulcy, ringed by the Moselle and the Jardin d'Amour. Mirrored in the water beside the Plan d'Eau, it is Metz's most photogenic riverside landmark and a prized concert venue for its acoustics.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Temple Neuf, Metz infobox

places.w: Roman baths near the ancient forum, unearthed during a 1987 car-park dig and now roofed by a great glass cube designed by Oswald M. Ungers — nicknamed 'Ungers' vitrine'. A cool, atmospheric walk over excavated Roman foundations; discovered a year too late to join Trier's UNESCO ensemble, though it would have deserved it.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Thermen am Viehmarkt infobox

places.ad: Rue du Marché-aux-Herbes, L-1728 Luxembourg (Ville Haute), Luxembourg
places.w: The official city residence of the Grand-Ducal family, with one of the finest façades in the country (Flemish Renaissance, 16th century). Guided tours run in summer, taking visitors into the Grand Duke's office, the dining room and the Salon des Rois.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Grand Ducal Palace)

places.ad: Place de la Constitution, L-1468 Luxembourg (Ville Haute), Luxembourg
places.w: The 'Golden Lady', a gilded Victory atop an obelisk on Place de la Constitution — a war memorial to Luxembourgers who served in the two World Wars and Korea, and one of the nation's most potent symbols, overlooking the Pétrusse valley.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Gëlle Fra)

places.w: The national museum of archaeology, history and art (Nationalmusée um Fëschmaart), on the old fish market. A rich sweep from prehistory to contemporary art, and the flagship of a State institute that also runs the Musée Dräi Eechelen.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (National Museum of Archaeology, History and Art)

places.n: Villa Vauban – Musée d'Art de la Ville de Luxembourg
places.ad: 18 Avenue Émile Reuter, L-2420 Luxembourg (Parc Municipal), Luxembourg
places.w: The city's art museum in an 1873 villa set in the municipal park — named for a Vauban fort once on the site. Dutch, French and Italian painting and sculpture (17th–19th c.) plus Luxembourg art from the 19th century on.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2223322 (Villa Vauban)

places.ad: 14 Rue du Saint-Esprit, L-1475 Luxembourg (Ville Haute), Luxembourg
places.w: The city history museum, threading a thousand years of Luxembourg's story through converted historic houses on the Rham escarpment, with a glass panoramic lift and views over the Grund.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Luxembourg City History Museum)

places.ad: 5 Park Dräi Eechelen, L-1499 Luxembourg (Kirchberg), Luxembourg
places.w: A fortress-and-history museum in the restored 18th-century Fort Thüngen on Kirchberg, its three rounded turrets — the 'Three Acorns' — surviving the 1867 demolition of the fortress. Traces the story of the fortress city from 1443 to 1903; faces Mudam across the moat.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Fort Thüngen)

places.w: A former Benedictine abbey in the Grund, begun 1606, restored and reopened in 2004 as neimënster — a cultural and conference centre with exhibitions, concerts and a riverside courtyard beneath the Bock cliffs.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Neimënster Abbey)

places.ad: Parc Pescatore / Pfaffenthal, Luxembourg City, Luxembourg
places.w: A free glass lift dropping 71 m in 30 seconds between the Ville Haute (by the Pescatore park) and the Pfaffenthal in the Alzette valley below, with sweeping views over the valley and viaducts. Open early morning to the small hours.

pv.src: Wikidata Q25583505 / EN Wikipedia (Pfaffenthal Panoramic Elevator)

places.ad: Place de la Constitution, L-1468 Luxembourg (Ville Haute), Luxembourg
places.w: The other great tunnel network of the UNESCO fortress (World Heritage since 1994), dug from 1644 under the Pétrusse valley and entered from Place de la Constitution. A 45-minute guided 'exploration' with immersive light-and-sound retraces four centuries of the fortress.

pv.src: Place de la Constitution entrance coordinate (visitluxembourg/kupi); consistent with Gëlle Fra Wikipedia pin

places.ad: Boulevard Roosevelt / Avenue de la Liberté, Luxembourg City, Luxembourg
places.w: A double-arched sandstone bridge of 1900–03 that once carried the largest stone arch in the world, spanning the Pétrusse between the Ville Haute and the Gare — an unofficial national symbol. A four-metre pedestrian-and-cycle 'Passerelle' now hangs beneath the deck.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Adolphe Bridge)

places.ad: Avenue Émile Reuter, Luxembourg City (Ville Haute/Limpertsberg), Luxembourg
places.w: The city's central English-style park, laid out by Édouard André on the old fortress glacis. Its great lawn, the Kinnekswiss ('king's meadow'), is the city's warm-weather gathering place and an open-air stage for summer concerts and the Winterlights market.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Municipal Park, Luxembourg City)

places.w: A farm plateau 60 years ago, now a showcase of contemporary architecture and seat of EU institutions — the European Court of Justice, Investment Bank and Court of Auditors — clustered with Mudam, the Philharmonie and public art around Place de l'Europe.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Kirchberg, Luxembourg)

places.ad: 41 Rue Notre-Dame, L-2240 Luxembourg (Ville Haute), Luxembourg
places.w: The country's leading contemporary-art centre since 1996, in a former bourgeois casino in the heart of the capital. An international programme leaning to younger artists, plus an art library, bookshop and café.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3019728 (Casino Luxembourg)

places.ad: Place Guillaume II, L-1648 Luxembourg (Ville Haute), Luxembourg
places.w: The great civic square of the Ville Haute, colloquially the 'Knuedler' after the knotted belt of the Franciscan friars whose monastery stood here. Dominated by the 1838 City Hall with its Trémont lions and the equestrian statue of Grand Duke William II; hosts the twice-weekly market.

pv.src: Wikidata Q359872 (Place Guillaume II)

places.ad: Bock / Montée de Clausen, Luxembourg City, Luxembourg
places.w: A signposted heritage trail — '1000 years of history in 180 minutes' — linking the Bock casemates, the Wenzel wall, the Alzette valley, the Grund and the Rham plateau, threading the UNESCO fortifications from the upper town down into the valley and back.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2714250 (Bock promontory, walk start)

places.ad: Avenue des Hauts Fourneaux, L-4362 Esch-sur-Alzette (Belval), Luxembourg
places.w: Two preserved blast furnaces of the former Esch-Belval steelworks (shut 1997), now the emblem of Luxembourg's Minett south and its 'Cité des Sciences'. Furnace A opens to a 40 m viewing platform; the Möllerei ore-storage hall is walkable. A hub of Esch2022, European Capital of Culture.

pv.src: Wikidata Q13101697 (Blast furnaces in Belval)

places.ad: Montée du Château, L-9710 Clervaux, Luxembourg
places.w: Edward Steichen's landmark 1955 photo exhibition — 503 images by 273 photographers from 68 countries, a post-war manifesto for peace — permanently installed in Clervaux Castle since 1994 and inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World register. Steichen was Luxembourg-born and wanted it to remain here.

pv.src: Wikipedia infobox (Clervaux Castle)

places.w: The largest castle in Luxembourg, a triangular fortress with an eleven-tower curtain wall standing 150 m above the Sûre in the Ardennes. Probably 10th-century, later Gothic-fortified; audio-guided in seven languages with panoramic valley views from the walls.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia (Bourscheid commune centre; castle-specific pin not found)

places.ad: 24 Rue du Château, L-6310 Beaufort, Luxembourg
places.w: Two castles in one wooded valley on the edge of the Mullerthal — the moated medieval ruins beside a Renaissance château — famous too for its home-made Cassero blackcurrant liqueur.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1010933 (Beaufort Castle, Luxembourg)

places.ad: Rue de Medernach, L-7620 Larochette, Luxembourg
places.w: An 11th-century castle on a crag above the little town of Larochette, home to several noble families. Large sections are restored, with exhibitions and reconstructed rooms and views over the Ernz Blanche valley.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1011703 (Larochette Castle)

places.ad: Rue Robert Goebbels, L-5444 Schengen, Luxembourg
places.w: On the tri-border Moselle where the 1985 Schengen Agreement was signed aboard the ship Princess Marie-Astrid, this museum (reopened 2025) tells the story of borderless Europe in a multilingual, interactive way — you can even print your own 'Schengen passport'.

pv.src: Wikidata Q13102046 (European Museum, Schengen)

places.w: An internationally respected museum in Diekirch, built around the Battle of the Bulge (winter 1944–45) fought in Luxembourg. Over 3,000 m² of vehicles, weaponry and life-size dioramas told even-handedly from American, German and civilian viewpoints.

pv.src: Wikidata Q478061 / EN Wikipedia (National Museum of Military History)

places.ad: 53 Route de Stadtbredimus, L-5570 Remich, Luxembourg
places.w: A sparkling-wine house just outside Remich, the 'Pearl of the Moselle', founded 1919. Guided tours walk nearly a kilometre of tunnels carved in the limestone (a constant, damp 12°C) and end with a tasting of Crémant de Luxembourg and Grand Premier Cru wines.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia (Remich town centre; caves-specific pin not found)

places.w: A slate-roofed village wrapped in a near-complete loop of the Sûre, below the ruins of one of the oldest castles in the country (first mentioned 927). In the heart of the Upper Sûre Nature Park by the Grand Duchy's largest lake; the castle is free to climb for valley views.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Esch-sur-Sûre Castle)

places.ad: Avenue des Bains, L-5601 Mondorf-les-Bains, Luxembourg
places.w: Luxembourg's thermal spa, an oasis of thermal baths, saunas and treatments in a 45-hectare wooded park near the Moselle. Its springs were discovered in 1841 and recognised for their health virtues from 1847.

pv.src: Official/mapping coordinate (mondorf.lu, Avenue des Bains)

places.ad: 115 Route du Vin, L-5416 Ehnen, Luxembourg
places.w: A wine museum in a typical group of pink-stucco Luxembourgish farm buildings in the round village of Ehnen, filled with old tools, presses and photographs of the Moselle wine trade, with a demonstration vineyard of the local grape varieties.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Wine Museum, Ehnen)

places.ad: 37 Rue de la Gare, L-9420 Vianden, Luxembourg
places.w: The riverside house where Victor Hugo lived during his 1871 exile and kept writing and sketching Vianden. A literary museum with his room, original artefacts, 70 information panels and hologram projections that bring the writer to life.

pv.src: Wikidata Q16764974 (Victor Hugo Literary Museum, Vianden)

places.ad: Rue du Sanatorium, L-9425 Vianden, Luxembourg
places.w: Luxembourg's only chairlift, running since 1958, floating 440 m above the Our valley in about ten minutes for magnificent views over the town and its great castle, with a café at the top station.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3546692 (Vianden chairlift)

places.ad: Château de Wiltz, L-9516 Wiltz, Luxembourg
places.w: A castle town in the Ardennes whose grand staircase becomes an open-air amphitheatre each June–July for the Festival de Wiltz (since 1953) — classical music, jazz, rock and theatre. The stables hold the National Museum of Brewing.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2244220 (Wiltz Castle)

places.ad: Route de Trèves, L-6793 Grevenmacher, Luxembourg
places.w: A tropical butterfly garden on the Moselle bank at Grevenmacher — hundreds of exotic butterflies of 40+ species flying free in a 28°C greenhouse, alongside quail, chameleons and turtles. Open April–October.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia/Apple Maps pin (Butterfly Garden, Grevenmacher)

places.ad: Rue des Caves, L-5471 Wellenstein, Luxembourg
places.w: Founded 1930, the largest single site of the Domaines Vinsmoselle cooperative and the biggest cellar in the Grand Duchy, the hub for shipping Vinsmoselle wines and crémant worldwide. Cellar tours and tastings year-round (except harvest), with a wine tavern and banqueting hall.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia (Wellenstein village centre)

places.w: The most imposing survivor of Metz's medieval walls — a double gate and bridge over the Seille, its two 13th-century round towers joined to 15th-century gun bastions. Named for the Teutonic Knights who kept a hospital nearby; classified a historic monument, restored and reopened in 2014 with free access and exhibitions.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Germans' Gate)

places.ad: 2 Rue du Haut Poirier, 57000 Metz, France
places.w: Named for the vanished palace of the kings of Austrasia, this 6,000 m² museum walks 2,000 years of Metz history with free admission — one of France's great Gallo-Roman collections (thermal baths preserved in situ, the Merten column, a Mithra altar), Merovingian sculpture from Saint-Pierre-aux-Nonnains, and a fine-arts gallery.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3329898 (Musée de la Cour d'Or)

places.ad: 1 Place du Général de Gaulle, 57000 Metz, France
places.w: Repeatedly voted France's most beautiful railway station, this 1908 Rhenish-Romanesque colossus (350 m long, the longest in France) was built under Kaiser Wilhelm II to stamp a German imperial identity on annexed Metz. Cathedral-like stained glass, a high tower, and carved arabesques crown the heart of the Quartier Impérial; a historic monument since 1975.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Metz-Ville station)

places.w: Ricardo Bofill's 1989 concert hall, now Arsenal-Jean-Marie-Rausch, whose Grande Salle is prized for exceptional acoustics — Rostropovich called it 'fantastic' at the opening. The complex folds in exhibition galleries and two remarkable monuments: the 4th-century Saint-Pierre-aux-Nonnains and the 12th-century Templars' Chapel.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2864371 (Arsenal de Metz)

places.ad: 4-5 Place de la Comédie, 57000 Metz, France
places.w: The oldest working opera house in France, inaugurated in 1752 on the elegant classical Place de la Comédie amid the water of the Moselle. Neo-classical and intimate, it is one of the last French houses to keep both a permanent choir and a ballet company.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Opéra-Théâtre de Metz Métropole)

places.w: A modest Outre-Seille church holding an outsized treasure: the last stained glass Jean Cocteau ever made, 24 windows across 14 bays created in 1961-63 — one of only three religious works of his life. Listed by Atlas Obscura among the places to see before you die.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2315622 (Église Saint-Maximin de Metz)

places.ad: 1 Rue de la Citadelle, 57000 Metz, France
places.w: Reputed the oldest church in France: a Gallo-Roman civil basilica of around 390 AD, turned into a church for a Benedictine convent in the 7th century — hence 'aux Nonnains'. Its white-limestone chancel is the most important preserved in France; today a monument and living cultural space beside the Arsenal.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Basilica of Saint-Pierre-aux-Nonnains)

places.w: Metz's most atmospheric old quarter, still medieval in feel below the towers of the Porte des Allemands — colombage houses, antiquarian and bookbinder shops, oriental grocers, and a young, bohemian crowd filling its bars, bistros and restaurants. The mid-September Foire à la Brocante is a local fixture.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3358654 (Outre-Seille)

places.w: The liveliest café square in the pedestrian heart of Metz, between Rue Fabert and Rue Ladoucette near the cathedral — terraces spilling out in the warm months, wooden chalets and mulled wine at Christmas.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2097855 (place Saint-Jacques, Metz)

places.n: Plan d'Eau de Metz & Lac aux Cygnes
places.w: A great artificial basin created in the 1970s where the Moselle splits the city — the Plan d'eau Saint-Symphorien on one bank, the Lac aux Cygnes park (a vestige of the old defensive moat) on the other. A favourite loop for walking, running and rowing, ringed by ramparts and the university's Île du Saulcy.

pv.src: Wikidata (Plan d'eau de Metz)

places.w: Four hectares of greenhouses, French parterres and romantic landscape founded in 1802 and moved here in 1865 around the 1719 Frescatelly summer pavilion — a century-old arboretum of ginkgos, sequoias and bald cypress, a rose garden and scent garden. Labelled 'Jardin remarquable' in 2025.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3162403 (Botanical garden of Metz)

places.ad: Rue du Fort de Queuleu, 57070 Metz, France
places.w: A fort built in 1868-70 to defend Metz that the Gestapo turned into an internment and transit camp in 1943-44, where 1,500-1,800 resisters and deportees were held before deportation. Now the regional memorial to resistance and deportation, with guided casemate visits and a wooded park open daily.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Fort de Queuleu)

places.w: A former convent on the Sainte-Croix hill turned cult music venue — an intimate vaulted 'Caveau', a chapel and an open cloister that made Metz a French home of jazz in the 1970s-80s, hosting Sonny Rollins and Archie Shepp, and still programming jazz, rock and chanson today.

pv.src: Wikidata Q3585932 (Église des Trinitaires de Metz)

places.w: One of the most beautiful squares in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1983, built 1752-55 for Stanislas Leszczynski, deposed king of Poland turned Duke of Lorraine. Emmanuel Héré's harmonious ensemble is framed by Jean Lamour's gilded wrought-iron gates and Guibal's fountains.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Place Stanislas)

places.w: The soaring neo-Gothic basilica of 1864-71 by Prosper Morey anchors Nancy's compact Ville Vieille — a medieval quarter of the Palais Ducal, Porte de la Craffe and cobbled lanes running between the old gate and the Arc Héré.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Saint-Epvre Basilica)

places.w: Nancy's 18th-century cathedral, begun in 1703 under Duke Léopold and continued by Stanislas, notable for its grand Dupont organ transformed by Cavaillé-Coll into a symphonic instrument of four keyboards and 65 stops. Free daily visits.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Nancy Cathedral)

places.w: The vast 1932 ossuary above the Verdun battlefield holds the remains of some 130,000 unidentified French and German soldiers, its national cemetery of 16,000 crosses stretching below. Where Mitterrand and Kohl clasped hands in 1984; part of the UNESCO WWI funerary and memorial sites since 2023, and the most visited monument in Lorraine.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Douaumont Ossuary)

places.ad: 1 Avenue du Corps Européen, 55100 Fleury-devant-Douaumont, France
places.w: A modern museum on the site of the destroyed village of Fleury dedicated to the 1916 Battle of Verdun and its soldiers — immersive reconstructions of the battlefield, personal testimony, film and a deep collection of period objects, the essential place to understand the war of attrition that cost 700,000 casualties.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Verdun Memorial)

places.ad: Avenue du 5e Régiment d'Artillerie à Pied, 55100 Verdun, France
places.w: Four kilometres of galleries dug beneath Verdun's citadel that became an underground city in 1916 — its ovens baking 28,000 rations a day and sheltering 2,000 men. Visited today in a self-guided car with augmented-reality glasses that reconstruct soldiers' daily life; here the Unknown Soldier was chosen in 1920.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2974403 (Verdun Citadel)

places.n: Musée de la Guerre de 1870 et de l'Annexion (Gravelotte)
places.w: Europe's only museum wholly devoted to the Franco-Prussian War and the 1871-1918 annexation of Alsace-Moselle, opened in 2014 on the very ground of the August 1870 battles of Gravelotte and Saint-Privat. Some 6,000 objects — paintings, sculpture, press, testimony — across the memorial site facing the Halle du Souvenir.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia (Gravelotte commune centre; museum in village)

places.w: An 11th-century fortress on a rocky spur above a Moselle bend at the three-borders point, one of the favourite residences of the Dukes of Lorraine and reputedly the only 11th-century castle with its walls, casemates and outer works still intact. Medieval re-enactments and craft workshops in season.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2971580 (Château des ducs de Lorraine)

places.w: A quadrangular 15th-century fortress with powerful corner towers near the three-borders region, begun around 1419 by Arnold VI of Sierck and nicknamed for the Duke of Marlborough of the famous song. Classified in 1930, it stages large seasonal art and culture exhibitions along a six-century discovery trail.

pv.src: Wikidata Q378453 (Château de Malbrouck)

places.w: A medieval bourg 6 km from Luxembourg, classed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1987 and nicknamed 'the little Lorraine Carcassonne' — still ringed by 700 m of 15th-century ramparts up to 9 m high, with cobbled lanes, the 1560 Maison des Baillis and a hilltop citadel.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox / Wikidata Q21939 (Rodemack)

places.w: The story of 'white gold' in the Saulnois, where salty springs were worked on a near-industrial scale from the Iron Age — 20,000 tonnes a year. Housed in a Vauban fortified gate, the Porte de France, and renewed with 3D headsets, tablets and a virtual-reality reconstruction of the citadel.

pv.src: Mapping/Wikidata Q3330543 (Musée départemental du sel de Marsal)

places.n: Musée départemental Georges de La Tour (Vic-sur-Seille)
places.w: In the Saulnois birthplace of the great Baroque master of candlelight, a museum built around its prize — La Tour's 'Saint-Jean-Baptiste dans le désert' — with 960 m² of French painting from the 17th to early 20th century (Le Brun, Stella, Valenciennes, Corot).

pv.src: Wikidata Q3330502 (Musée départemental Georges de La Tour)

places.w: The 12th-century keep of Thionville's feudal castle — its odd name a garbling of the Frankish for 'tower at the well' — now the municipal museum, telling the town's story from prehistory to the Renaissance across eight thematic rooms, near the market-square belfry and its two-tonne bell 'Grosse Suzanne'.

pv.src: Wikidata Q22959920 (Tour aux Puces)

places.w: Between Metz and Thionville, one of France's densest leisure clusters set in forest — a European-scale zoo of nearly 2,000 animals across 18 hectares, France's only indoor ski slope, an aquarium, an Olympic ice rink and the Thermapolis thermal baths on iron-rich hot springs.

pv.src: Mapping pin (Zoo d'Amnéville, heart of the Cité des Loisirs)

places.w: The largest Maginot Line artillery fortress, built 1929-35 — nineteen surface blocks linked by kilometres of underground galleries, ammunition stores, kitchens and a power plant, reached on an electric train inside the rock. Two-hour guided visits at a constant 12°C, culminating in the combat blocks and their turrets.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Ouvrage Hackenberg)

places.n: Moulin de la Blies – Musée des Techniques Faïencières (Sarreguemines)
places.ad: 125 Avenue de la Blies, 57200 Sarreguemines, France
places.w: Voted the French people's 9th favourite monument in 2015, the former paste-preparation mill of the great Sarreguemines pottery (1825-1969) now shows the machines and tools of faience-making, wrapped in the seven-part Jardin des Faïenciers laid out over the industrial ruins on the Blies riverbank.

pv.src: Wikidata Q20971749 (Moulin de la Blies)

places.n: Musée des Émaux et Faïences de Longwy
places.w: In Longwy-Haut, the city of the famous crackle-glaze enamels, a museum in a former military bakery tracing two crafts — faience made from 1798 and the celebrated cloisonné-style enamels from the 1870s — including the 200-piece Vernaujou-Brunet collection of Longwy enamels.

pv.src: Wikidata Q23640256 (Longwy Enamels Museum)

places.w: The centre of medieval Trier since 958, ringed by Renaissance, Baroque and Gothic facades (Steipe, Rotes Haus), the Petrusbrunnen and the Gothic Judenpforte. Its Marktkreuz — set up by Archbishop Heinrich I. in 958 on a Carolingian palmette capital — is thought to be Europe's oldest surviving medieval market cross (the original is now in the Stadtmuseum Simeonstift).

pv.src: Wikidata Q897212 (Hauptmarkt Trier)

places.w: An early-Gothic patrician tower-house of about 1230 on the Simeonstraße between the Porta Nigra and the Hauptmarkt, one of Trier's most important secular medieval buildings. Its original door sat high on the first floor, reached by a removable ladder for defence — a rare survival of a fortified townhouse.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1257914 (Dreikönigenhaus, Trier)

places.w: One of Germany's most important archaeological museums (founded 1877), telling the story of Augusta Treverorum with a Roman collection — mosaics, frescoes, sculpture, the Neumagen wine ship and one of the world's largest Roman gold-coin hoards — among the finest north of the Alps. Part of the 'Zentrum der Antike' with the Roman monuments.

pv.src: Wikidata Q885326 (Rheinisches Landesmuseum Trier)

places.w: Trier's city museum, housed in the Romanesque cloister buildings of the former Simeonstift right beside the Porta Nigra. It shows the city's art and history from the Middle Ages to the 21st century — paintings, sculpture, applied arts and the original medieval Marktkreuz.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2327696 (City Museum Simeonstift, Trier)

places.w: The bishops' cathedral and diocesan museum, best known for the sensational Roman ceiling fresco — a 10-metre painting from a Constantinian palace that lay shattered underground for almost 1,700 years — reassembled here, alongside Christian art from two millennia.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1954513 (Museum am Dom Trier)

places.w: Germany's oldest bridge and part of Trier's UNESCO World Heritage Roman monuments: the five surviving mid-2nd-century basalt piers (AD 144–152) still carry road traffic across the Mosel today, nearly 1,900 years on. Best viewed from the riverbank with the Mariensäule on the far hill.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Roman Bridge, Trier)

places.w: A narrow medieval lane entered from the Hauptmarkt through the Judenpforte, the heart of Trier's Jewish quarter from the 11th century until the expulsion of 1418. The gate structure dates to 1219 (rebuilt 1607/08) with Renaissance houses above — an atmospheric survival of the old town's medieval street pattern.

pv.src: Wikidata Q897225 (Judengasse, Trier)

places.w: A 40-metre Marian column of 1866 standing about 150 m above the city on the Pulsberg on the left bank of the Mosel. The terrace beneath it is one of Trier's classic viewpoints, taking in the whole old town, the Dom and the Roman bridge below.

pv.src: Wikidata Q464654 (Mariensäule Trier; arcminute-rounded)

places.w: A hillside viewpoint above the Roman amphitheatre, set among vineyards on the Petrisberg (the old Martinsberg). The terrace gives the finest panorama over Trier's old town and the Mosel valley — a favourite spot for sunset and, in season, a walk down through the vines.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2551878 (Wasserturm auf dem Petrisberg, adjacent landmark on the Petrisberg summit)

places.ad: Burg Landshut, Am Burgberg, 54470 Bernkastel-Kues, Germany
places.w: A late-13th-century archbishops' castle ruin on Roman foundations, towering over Bernkastel-Kues. Gutted by fire in 1692 and long a romantic ruin, it reopened with a café-restaurant and terrace after restoration; the walk up the vineyard rewards you with the classic panorama over the twin town and its Mosel loop.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1012833 (Burg Landshut)

places.w: The Gothic almshouse founded in 1458 by the philosopher-cardinal Nicholas of Cusa (born in Kues) for 33 poor men — still a home for the elderly, Germany's oldest. Its chapel, cloister and, above all, the medieval library of some 314 manuscripts and Cusa's astronomical instruments make it a treasure of the Mosel.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2321933 (Cusanusstift / St. Nikolaus-Hospital)

places.w: For decades one of West Germany's best-kept secrets: a Cold War bunker hidden beneath two ordinary-looking houses where the Bundesbank stored up to 15 billion Deutsche Mark of emergency replacement currency (1964–1988) against a feared Soviet hyperinflation attack. A museum since 2016 with 60-minute guided tours 30 m underground.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia infobox (Bundesbank bunker)

places.w: Cochem's much-loved chairlift, gliding up over the vineyards to the Pinnerkreuz viewpoint at 255 m, where the Reichsburg, the town and the sweeping Mosel bend lie spread out below. One of the town's most popular outings.

pv.src: Mapping pin (Pinnerkreuz lookout, upper station of the Cochemer Sesselbahn)

places.w: Around 2,000 Buddha figures from across Asia displayed over 4,000 m² inside the old Julius Kayser sekt cellar — the only winery in the world built in full Jugendstil style, designed by Berlin architect Bruno Möhring. A striking pairing of Art Nouveau architecture and Far-Eastern art on the Mosel bank, with a roof-garden river view.

pv.src: Wikidata Q15790167 (Buddha-Museum Traben-Trarbach)

places.w: The ruin of the 14th-century Grevenburg above Traben-Trarbach, seat of the 'Hintere Grafschaft Sponheim', besieged six times and finally blown up by the French in 1734. A short steep climb reaches the surviving gate and a grand panorama over the twin town and the Mosel.

pv.src: Wikidata Q885158 (Grevenburg)

places.w: The town's landmark bridge gate of 1899, a Jugendstil gatehouse by Bruno Möhring guarding the Mosel crossing — a reminder that Traben-Trarbach was, around 1900, the second-largest wine-trading centre in Europe after Bordeaux. The starting point for a walk past the town's Art-Nouveau villas.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia (Traben-Trarbach town centre; gate stands at south end of Mosel bridge)

places.ad: Burg Metternich, Im Mühlenthal 62, 56814 Beilstein, Germany
places.w: Rick Steves' favourite Mosel village — the 'Sleeping Beauty of the Mosel', a near-untouched huddle of half-timbered houses, the Klostertreppe and a market square, with barely 140 residents. Above it stand the ruins of Burg Metternich, whose five-sided keep gives a beautiful view over the Cochem Mosel loops.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1013124 (Metternich Castle, Beilstein)

places.n: Karmeliterkirche St. Josef & Schwarze Madonna, Beilstein
places.w: The Baroque Carmelite monastery church above Beilstein's Klostertreppe, home to the venerated 'Wondrous Black Madonna' that makes the tiny village a pilgrimage site. Worth the climb for the interior and the view back over the rooftops to the Mosel.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1734063 / de.wikipedia Karmeliterkirche St. Josef (Beilstein) infobox (50°6'37.1"N 7°14'24.7"E)

places.w: The wine town of Zell, famous worldwide for its 'Zeller Schwarze Katz' (Black Cat) Riesling — the legend of a barrel guarded by a hissing black cat is told at the Schwarze-Katz-Brunnen on the promenade. A steep trail from the fountain climbs to the Collis-Turm, whose terrace overlooks Zell and its Mosel bend.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia/Wikidata Q187500 (Zell (Mosel) town centre; Schwarze-Katz fountain at the marketplace)

places.w: Neumagen-Dhron calls itself Germany's oldest wine village, thanks to the world-famous Roman wine ship carved on a 3rd-century merchant's tomb found here in 1878. A full-size, seaworthy replica, the Stella Noviomagi, has been moored since 2007 and runs river trips past the steep vineyards it once carried wine through.

pv.src: EN Wikipedia/Wikidata Q552474 (Neumagen-Dhron town centre; ship on the Mosel riverbank)

places.w: A rare thing: a near-20-metre waterfall in the middle of a town. The Leukbach tumbles between half-timbered houses and Baroque facades in Saarburg's old town, once driving a row of mills; below it the Staden, the oldest quarter, runs down to the Saar. On the Saar edge of the Mosel-Saar wine country.

pv.src: kuladig.de / outdooractive Wasserfall Saarburg (Leukbach) place coordinate

places.w: Europe's steepest vineyard — slopes up to about 65° of pure slate above the Mosel between Bremm and Ediger-Eller, worked entirely by hand. A roughly 5 km via-ferrata trail, secured in places with steel cables, ladders and rungs, threads through the vines to dizzying river views; the Riesling grown here is legendary.

pv.src: de.wikipedia/en.wikipedia Calmont (hill) infobox summit (50°06'33"N 7°07'25"E)

places.w: The world's only completely preserved ironworks from the heyday of industrialisation, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1994 — the first industrial site ever so honoured. Walk the 240 m charging platform and climb the 40 m blast-furnace viewing deck; today it doubles as a monumental venue for exhibitions and festivals.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Voelklingen Ironworks infobox

places.w: Saarland's signature landscape: the river doubling back on itself in a great loop 180 m below the free Cloef viewpoint at Orscholz — the most photographed view in the state.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1102142 (Cloef viewpoint)

places.w: A treetop walkway opened in 2016 above the Cloef, winding on gentle ramps to a 42 m tower with a fresh, elevated angle on the Saar loop — an easy family favourite paired with the viewpoint.

pv.src: Wikidata Q27478902 (Treetop Walk Saarschleife)

places.w: Saarbrücken's landmark and the crown of baroque master builder Friedrich Joachim Stengel's 'Ludwigsplatz' ensemble — reckoned among Germany's most important Protestant churches alongside Dresden's Frauenkirche.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Ludwigskirche (Saarbruecken) infobox

places.w: The lively heart of Saarbrücken — a pedestrian old-town square of boutiques, bistros and pubs around Stengel's 1759 baroque market fountain, with a sight-axis to the castle across the Saar.

pv.src: Wikidata Q15848504 (St. Johanner Markt)

places.w: Stengel's 18th-century baroque palace on the sandstone cliff above the Saar, its centre rebuilt in glass-and-steel by Gottfried Böhm; beneath and beside it the Historisches Museum Saar tells the region's turbulent border history.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Saarbruecken Castle infobox

places.w: Two and a half centuries of ceramics inside the baroque former Benedictine abbey that is Villeroy & Boch's headquarters in Mettlach — 2,000 m² of tableware, historical scenes and a reconstructed 1892 milk shop, plus the outlet and abbey park.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Mettlach / Abtei Mettlach - abbey is the town centre on the Saar (Saaruferstrasse)

places.w: A ~50 ha park laid out in 1960 on the former Westwall fortifications right on the German-French border — themed gardens, lakes, a little cable car and the Gulliver miniature world; a symbol of post-war reconciliation and the city's favourite green space.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1201760 (Deutsch-Franzoesischer Garten)

places.w: In the Kreisständehaus beside the palace: a high-calibre gallery of Renaissance-to-19th-century painting, 17th-century Dutch landscape and still life, and Nassau-Saarbrücken portraits, silver and porcelain — the historic wing of the Saarlandmuseum.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Schlossplatz/Saarbruecken Castle; Alte Sammlung at Schlossplatz 16, adjacent to the castle

places.w: The hexagonal fortress town Louis XIV had Vauban and Thomas de Choisy build from 1680, its casemates now housing restaurants and its water-filled moats turned to parkland. The green, café-lined old town keeps a distinctly French flair.

pv.src: OpenStreetMap Way 71892595 (Vauban-Insel, Saarlouis) via mapcarta

places.w: One of western Germany's finest late-Gothic hall churches, holding the relics of St Wendelin and, from 1462, a stone pulpit donated by Nikolaus von Kues said to be Germany's second oldest — the jewel of St. Wendel's restored old town.

pv.src: Structurae / de.wikipedia Wendalinusbasilika (St. Wendel)

places.w: A restored medieval castle on the wooded ridge inside the Saar loop, reached on shaded footpaths — a classic Saarschleife excursion pairing ruins-turned-museum with river views.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1013137 (Burg Montclair)

places.w: Nicknamed 'la Lanterne du Bon Dieu' for the largest expanse of stained glass in France — some 6,500 m² spanning the 13th to 21st centuries, including windows by Marc Chagall. Metz's soaring Gothic landmark.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Metz Cathedral infobox

places.ad: 1 Parvis des Droits de l'Homme, 57000 Metz, France
places.w: The Pompidou's first regional offshoot and Metz's cultural magnet, under a spectacular woven roof by Shigeru Ban and Jean de Gastines. Major modern and contemporary art shows draw on the national collection.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Centre Pompidou-Metz infobox

places.w: The Wilhelmine 'new town' around the monumental Gare de Metz, an eclectic parade of neo-Romanesque, neo-Gothic and Jugendstil built during the German annexation — a UNESCO-candidate ensemble unique in France.

pv.src: Tourisme Metz / ViaMichelin POI (Quartier Imperial, Place du General de Gaulle)

places.ad: Place de la Cathédrale, 57000 Metz, France
places.w: One of France's oldest and grandest covered markets, on the cathedral square in a neo-classical hall begun in 1785. Over 40 stalls of Lorraine produce — quiche, pâté lorrain, Munster, tomme de Moselle, charcuterie — make it the city's larder.

pv.src: Wikidata Q17073035 (Covered Market, Metz)

places.n: Musée de la Faïence de Sarreguemines
places.w: The story of the great Sarreguemines faience works, in the villa of its 19th-century director around a sumptuous 1880 Winter Garden classified a Monument Historique. Majolica, tableware and decorative ceramics fill the recently renovated rooms.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Sarreguemines (town) 49.11/7.07; museum at 16 rue Poincare

places.w: Vauban's dramatic 17th-century citadel riding a sandstone glacis near the German border, famed for holding out 230 days in the 1870 war. An audio-guided underground circuit, the 'Men in the War of 1870' museum and a panorama over the Northern Vosges, with the Jardin pour la Paix below.

pv.src: Wikidata Q206240 (Citadelle de Bitche)

places.w: The honeycomb of tunnels and gun galleries carved into the Bock promontory where Count Siegfried founded Luxembourg in 963 — the core of the fortifications that earned the old town its UNESCO listing, with dizzying views over the Alzette valley.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Bock (Luxembourg) infobox

places.ad: Chemin de la Corniche, 1945 Luxembourg, Luxembourg
places.w: Called 'Europe's most beautiful balcony' — a rampart-top promenade along the old city walls with sweeping views down to the Grund and the Alzette. The essential first walk in the capital, and free.

pv.src: OpenStreetMap Way 82537050 (Chemin de la Corniche) - rampart walk between Bock and Grund

places.w: The picturesque lower town on the river beneath the cliffs, reached by a free rock-cut lift — cobbled lanes, the Neumünster abbey cultural centre and riverside terraces, part of the UNESCO old town.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Grund, Luxembourg infobox

places.w: The Grand Duchy's only cathedral, a late-Gothic church built by the Jesuits in 1613-21 with Renaissance and Baroque touches, the venerated 'Consoler of the Afflicted' and the crypt of the grand-ducal family.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Notre-Dame Cathedral, Luxembourg infobox

places.n: Mudam – Musée d'Art Moderne Grand-Duc Jean
places.w: Luxembourg's museum of modern art on the Kirchberg plateau, in a light-filled building by I. M. Pei set on the ruins of Fort Thüngen. Bold rotating shows of international and local artists.

pv.src: en.wikipedia MUDAM infobox

places.w: Christian de Portzamparc's colonnaded 2005 concert hall on the Kirchberg, its Grand Auditorium counted among the world's finest for acoustics — architecture worth seeing even without a ticket.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Philharmonie Luxembourg infobox

places.w: One of Europe's finest Romanesque-Gothic castles, magnificently rebuilt on a ridge above the Our valley, with the Victor Hugo house-museum in the fairy-tale town below — the country's most impressive fortress.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Vianden Castle infobox

places.ad: Parvis de la Basilique, 6486 Echternach, Luxembourg
places.w: Luxembourg's oldest town, grown around St Willibrord's 7th-century Benedictine abbey and basilica, with Roman traces, medieval walls and a lake. Its Whit-Tuesday Hopping Procession is UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Abbey of Echternach infobox

places.w: 'Luxembourg's Little Switzerland' — a 112 km trail through dense forest, gorges and dramatic rock formations, its emblem the triple-cascade Schiessentümpel waterfall with its little stone bridge.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2529613 (Scheissendempel/Schiessentuempel waterfall, Mullerthal)

places.w: The best-preserved Roman city gate north of the Alps, raised around 170 AD as the north entrance to Augusta Treverorum. The blackened sandstone landmark of Germany's oldest city and part of Trier's UNESCO ensemble.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Porta Nigra infobox

places.w: Germany's oldest bishop's church — a Romanesque cathedral on Roman foundations, holding the Holy Robe — joined by the Liebfrauenkirche, one of the earliest Gothic churches in Germany. Both are inscribed on the UNESCO list.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Trier Cathedral infobox

places.w: The vast 4th-century imperial baths, among the largest in the Roman Empire, their soaring brick apses and underground service tunnels open to explore — a highlight of Trier's Roman UNESCO monuments.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Trier Imperial Baths infobox

places.w: Constantine's early-4th-century throne hall — the largest surviving single-room structure from Roman antiquity, now a Protestant church. Its scale is astonishing; part of the UNESCO ensemble.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Aula Palatina infobox

places.w: The Roman amphitheatre built into the Petrisberg slope around the 2nd century, once seating over 20,000 and doubling as part of the city wall — its arena and cellar vaults still walkable. Part of Trier's UNESCO monuments.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Trier Amphitheater infobox

places.w: The baroque townhouse where Karl Marx was born in 1818, now a museum on his life, work and worldwide impact run by the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Karl Marx House infobox

places.w: A neo-Gothic fantasy castle perched over 100 m above a Mosel bend at Cochem — rebuilt in the 19th century on medieval foundations and one of the most photogenic sights on the river.

pv.src: Wikidata Q506465 (Reichsburg Cochem)

places.w: The postcard heart of the Middle Mosel — a market square framed by leaning half-timbered houses beneath the ruined Burg Landshut, birthplace of Nikolaus von Kues and gateway to the Bernkasteler Doctor vineyards.

pv.src: en.wikipedia Bernkastel-Kues (town) - historic Marktplatz, old town

places.w: A completed-around-1390 Gothic three-aisled basilica ranked among the most important architectural monuments of the German southwest, holding the carved gravestones of the Counts of Nassau-Saarbrücken and crowned by a Stengel cupola of 1746. It anchors St. Arnual, the medieval 'village within the city' with its own market square.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Stift Sankt Arnual infobox / Wikidata Q1422153 (tower 49°13'06.5"N 7°01'05.8"E)

places.w: The Catholic parish church of the old St. Johann quarter, a 1754-58 baroque work by Friedrich Joachim Stengel just off the market square. A quieter Stengel counterpart to the Ludwigskirche, elevated to a minor basilica for its architectural and historical rank.

pv.src: DE Wikipedia/Wikidata Q810112 (Basilika St. Johann, Saarbrücken)

places.w: The oldest surviving bridge in all of Saarland, a ~200 m stone arch bridge of 1546/47 spanning the Saar between the baroque castle and the St. Johanner Markt. A free, central walk with the castle rock on one bank and the old town on the other.

pv.src: Wikidata Q435413 (Alte Brücke, Saarbrücken)

places.w: One of the leading art museums of southwest Germany, its holdings running from Impressionism and the Berlin Secession through German Expressionism, the École de Paris and Informel to the present, with a sculpture garden. The modern wing of the Saarlandmuseum, recently enlarged by a new pavilion.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Saarlandmuseum infobox (49°13'48.28"N 6°59'57.751"E)

places.w: Saarland's four-division state theatre (opera, drama, dance, concert), mounting around 30 new productions a year in some 700 performances for more than 200,000 visitors. Its monumental 1938 house on Schillerplatz overlooking the Saar is a landmark in its own right.

pv.src: EN/DE Wikipedia infobox (Theater Saarbrücken / Saarländisches Staatstheater)

places.w: Europe's largest man-made red-sandstone caves, twelve storeys of vaulted halls and kilometres of galleries dug from the 11th to 17th centuries beneath the ruins of Hohenburg fortress. About 800 m across the top three walkable levels are open, glowing in bands of ochre and red.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Schlossberghöhlen / Wikidata Q2244435 (49°19'16.0"N 7°20'35.9"E)

places.w: An open-air archaeological museum on the excavated Roman vicus of Schwarzenacker, a country town of some 2,000 people that lived from about the birth of Christ until its destruction by the Alemanni in 275 AD. Reconstructed streets and houses, plus a baroque garden, bring the Roman Saar to life; combine it with the Homburg caves.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Römermuseum Schwarzenacker / Wikidata Q2179623 (49.282553, 7.315982)

places.w: A 30 m walkable steel landmark crowning the ~150 m mining dump above Ensdorf, opened in 2016 to commemorate the end of Saar coal mining (the last pit closed here in 2012). 132 steps climb through its two pylons to a free viewing platform that seems to change shape as you move — a symbol of the region's transformation.

pv.src: Wikidata Q24531242 Saarpolygon (49°19'4.8"N 6°47'6.0"E)

places.w: The 8-hectare wolf park that made Merzig the 'city of wolves', home to around 20 European grey, polar, Canadian timber and Mongolian wolves in wide open enclosures. Founded by behavioural researcher Werner Freund, who lived for decades 'as a wolf among wolves'; free to walk through, with a monthly public feeding and talk.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Wolfspark Werner Freund infobox (49°28'14"N 6°38'29"E)

places.w: A luxurious Roman villa whose entrance hall keeps the largest and best-preserved mosaic floor north of the Alps — over 160 m² of some three million stones showing gladiators, beast-hunts and musicians of the amphitheatre, found by a farmer in 1852. One of the outstanding works of Roman mosaic art anywhere.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Römische Villa in Nennig / Wikidata Q76637550 (49°31'43.853"N 6°23'4.967"E)

places.w: At 120 hectares the largest recreational lake in southwest Germany, in the wooded St. Wendel uplands, with free bathing beaches, sailing and surfing, a lakeside path and the Bosaarium wave pool. Opened 1979 and now flanked by a Center Parcs holiday village — the state's summer playground.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Bostalsee / Wikidata Q894539 (49°34'5.9"N 7°4'18.8"E)

places.w: Reckoned the most beautiful baroque town in Saarland, built up under Countess Marianne von der Leyen in the heart of the UNESCO Bliesgau Biosphere Reserve — a fine ensemble of the Schlosskirche, town hall, Paradeplatz and burgher houses. A compact, walkable old town with Kneipp-spa calm.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2244565 Schlosskirche Blieskastel, adjacent to Paradeplatz / baroque old-town ensemble anchor (49°14'13.55"N 7°15'15.94"E)

places.w: A roughly 4,000-year-old menhir standing 6.58 m tall on the hill above Blieskastel — the largest menhir in Central Europe and the landmark of the baroque town. Re-erected after wartime damage, it is the goal of the panoramic Mariannenweg walk.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Gollenstein / Wikidata Q593489 (N 49°14.677' E 7°14.974')

places.w: A leafy hillside zoo above the city with around 1,000 animals of 100 species, from big cats and primates to a walk-through aviary — a long-standing family outing on the St. Arnual side of Saarbrücken.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Saarbrücker Zoo / Wikidata Q2209172 (main entrance 49°13'50.9"N 7°2'22.6"E)

places.w: Saarbrücken's neo-Gothic town hall of 1897-1900 by Georg von Hauberrisser (architect of Munich's town hall), with a 54 m tower, festive hall and richly ornamented façade. The square in front and the building's Von-Uexküll murals reward a look inside.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2132615 Rathaus St. Johann Saarbrücken (49°14'5"N 6°59'47"E)

places.w: Inside the Gothic castle church below Saarbrücker Schloss: a collection of religious art from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, with the baroque princely tombs of Nassau-Saarbrücken and vivid modern stained glass by Georg Meistermann. The third site of the Saarlandmuseum.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Schlosskirche (Saarbrücken) / Wikidata Q2244579 (49.231133, 6.991141)

places.n: Botanischer Garten der Universität des Saarlandes — CLOSED
places.ad: Universität des Saarlandes Campus, 66123 Saarbrücken, Germany
places.w: A 25,000 m² botanical garden on the western edge of the university campus with five greenhouses of plants from different climate zones and an attached medicinal-plant museum. A free, quiet green detour when visiting the Saarbrücken campus.

pv.src: en/de.wikipedia Botanischer Garten der Universität des Saarlandes / Wikidata Q824180 (49°15'16.2"N 7°2'16.1"E)
pv.ss: en.wikipedia: garden closed to the public 1 April 2016

places.w: A fairy-tale red-sandstone villa of 1858 in central Merzig, its asymmetrical turrets and bay windows housing a cultural-history museum and set in the Paul-Schneider sculpture park. A relaxed cultural stop in the Saarschleifenland.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Schloss Fellenberg / Wikidata Q2240971 (49.44584, 6.64592)

places.ad: Stausee Losheim, 66679 Losheim am See, Germany
places.w: A 1974 reservoir ringed by beaches, a lakeside promenade and the start of premium 'Traumschleifen' hiking loops in the Saar-Hunsrück nature park; a heritage steam railway runs to Merzig. An easy nature-and-swimming day out in the northwest of the state.

pv.src: Wikidata Q2334716 Stausee Losheim (49.5183, 6.7328)

places.w: One of Germany's most important baroque square ensembles, laid out from 1762 by Friedrich Joachim Stengel around the Ludwigskirche — church and surrounding palais planned as a single stage set. It was on Germany's UNESCO tentative list and appears on the Saarland 2-euro coin.

pv.src: de/en.wikipedia Ludwigskirche (Saarbrücken) / Wikidata Q539324, centrepiece of the Ludwigsplatz Stengel ensemble (49°13'58"N 6°59'11"E)

places.w: A woodland zoo near the centre of Neunkirchen with over 600 animals of around 120 species, a well-regarded family destination on the eastern side of the Saarland.

pv.src: laengengrad-breitengrad.de / familienausflug.info published GPS for Neunkircher Zoo, Zoostraße 25 (49.345890, 7.204900) — no Wikipedia infobox coordinate

places.w: A model-garden park created in 1951 (during Saarland's post-war French-protectorate years) with a rose garden, alpine and heather gardens, ponds and a museum-and-observation tower. A gentle, nostalgic place for a stroll, and the new home of the old Saarbrücken 'Gulliver World' miniatures.

pv.src: outdooractive/touren.saarland Blumengarten Bexbach place coordinate (49.341507, 7.259104)

places.w: The state's mining museum, founded 1934, telling the whole story of Saar hard-coal mining from a 40 m panorama tower down into an extensive walk-through demonstration mine with machines and support types from different eras. The definitive place to grasp the industry that shaped the region.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1303084 Saarländisches Bergbaumuseum (Hindenburgturm) (49°20'57.8"N 7°15'33.8"E)

places.w: Germany's newspaper museum, opened 2004 in a former economic building of Wadgassen Abbey, with some 4,000 objects on the history, technology and distribution of the press and a large specialist library. A niche but well-made museum on the story of print.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Deutsches Zeitungsmuseum / Wikidata Q16739189 (49°16'15.258"N 6°47'30.844"E)

places.w: Reckoned the oldest monastery on German soil, with roots in the 7th century on a Roman villa site and an early-Gothic abbey church of 1230-60. Newly fitted with 30 luminous windows by Mahbuba Maqsoodi and three towering choir windows by Gerhard Richter — a pilgrimage for lovers of contemporary church art, with abbey beer, wine and honey to take home.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Benediktinerabtei St. Mauritius (Tholey) / Abteikirche Tholey infobox (49.481384, 7.031345)

places.w: A remarkably intact small old town of Renaissance and baroque houses in the former residence of the Counts of Nassau-Saarbrücken, marked by the 15th-century Zibbelkapp tower and Stengel's pavilion and widow's palace. Best explored on one of the costumed night-watchman tours.

pv.src: outdooractive Historische Altstadt von Ottweiler / Schlossplatz place coordinate (49°24'13.5"N 7°09'40.5"E)

places.w: The German Gate of Vauban's fortress city, flanked by Prussian casemates of 1824-29 that once quartered soldiers and horses and today house a row of restaurants locals call 'Saarland's longest bar', with 1870-war cannons on the walls. The atmospheric fortified edge of French-flavoured Saarlouis.

pv.src: de.wikipedia Deutsches Tor (Saarlouis) / Wikidata Q1206067 (49°19'0.5"N 6°44'55.7"E)

places.w: Nancy's Art Nouveau temple, opened in 1911 opposite the station and a Monument Historique — Gruber stained glass, Majorelle furniture, Daum lamps, aproned waiters. A grand seafood brasserie of the École de Nancy where the signature 'Tout Nancy' dessert stacks the city's macaron, bergamot and mirabelle. The definitive Nancy dining room.

pv.src: fr.wikipedia Brasserie Excelsior (monument historique infobox)

places.w: A MICHELIN-Guide address 300 m from Place Stanislas where chef Hervé Fourrière cooks a personal, classically grounded cuisine with a strong hand on fish and produce, in an elegant contemporary-baroque room. A long-running Nancy gastronomic name.

pv.src: restovisio.com venue POI (31 rue Gambetta, Nancy)

places.w: The keeper of the real Nancy macaron — a crackled, almond-only biscuit whose recipe descends from two Benedictine sisters in 1793 — plus the IGP-protected bergamotes de Nancy, mirabelle specialities and pâtes de fruits. A Living-Heritage (EPV) confectioner near Place Stanislas.

pv.src: mappy POI (fr.mappy.com/poi/4d6c96d1fc692507e11611d7) / pagesjaunes for 21 rue Gambetta - coordinate stated in result text

places.w: A café-brasserie institution on Place Stanislas since the 1850s, named for a Napoleonic general and reopened in 2024 with its mirrors and velvet intact. Lorraine classics — quiche, mirabelle — and a terrace on the finest square in France; a favourite lunch of critic Gilles Pudlowski.

pv.src: findlatitudeandlongitude geocode of exact address 1 Place Stanislas, Nancy

places.w: Strasbourg's historic haute-cuisine address, open since 1840 and once a three-star under Émile Jung — the stuffed crocodile in the window a Napoleonic souvenir. Now a MICHELIN one-star (Relais & Châteaux) where chef Romain Brillat balances classicism and refinement in the city centre.

pv.src: mappy.fr venue POI (10 rue de l'Outre, Strasbourg)

places.w: The most famous winstub in Strasbourg, a tavern since 1873 that took Yvonne Haller's name in 1959 — checked cloths, tight tables and the full Alsatian canon: choucroute, coq au Riesling, bibeleskäs, glazed kouglof. A MICHELIN-Guide winstub a step from the cathedral.

pv.src: restovisio/mappy venue POI (10 rue du Sanglier, Strasbourg)

places.w: A warm winstub institution on the picturesque Place du Marché-aux-Cochons-de-Lait, plating generous Alsatian cooking — a five-garnish choucroute, spaetzle, vol-au-vent, fried Munster — sometimes with a creative twist. Listed by Gault&Millau.

pv.src: mapcarta W39652757 centroid of Place du Marché-aux-Cochons-de-Lait (small named square the venue is on, not a town centroid)

places.w: The most photographed house in Petite France — a galleried 1572 half-timbered tannery that has held a winstub since 1949 — serving the Alsatian repertoire (choucroute, tarte flambée, coq au Riesling) over the canals of the Ill. Setting and plate in one.

pv.src: strasbourg.eu / archi-wiki venue entry (Maison des Tanneurs, monument historique)

places.ad: 16 Place de la Cathédrale, 67000 Strasbourg, France
places.w: 'The most beautiful house in Strasbourg', a Gothic-and-Renaissance timber landmark of 1427-1589 at the cathedral's foot, listed since 1929 and painted inside by Léo Schnug. A destination brasserie for Alsatian cooking, above all its choucroute of three fishes.

pv.src: Wikipedia/Wikidata Q661723 Kammerzell House infobox

places.ad: 6 Rue du Tonnelet Rouge, 67000 Strasbourg, France
places.w: The address that gave the tarte flambée its cult revival — thin, wood-fired flammekueche from surrounding farms' produce in a no-frills, buzzy room, opened by Régis Nombret in 2010 (now with a second Binchstub on Place Broglie). A local favourite for the real thing.

pv.src: mappy/yandex venue POI (6 rue du Tonnelet Rouge, Strasbourg)

places.w: A pâtisserie-chocolaterie and salon de thé in the centre, prized for its kougelhopf (sweet and the bacon-walnut savoury version), Alsatian tarts and chocolates. A reliable stop for the region's baking canon; recommended by Gault&Millau and the Alsace tourist board.

pv.src: petitfute/mappy venue POI (Pâtisserie Christian, Strasbourg cathedral quarter)

places.n: Cave Historique des Hospices de Strasbourg
places.w: A 1,200 m² medieval wine cellar under the city hospital, built 1393-1395 and still ageing Alsace wine — home to a 1472 vintage, one of the oldest wines in the world. Taste and buy Riesling, Gewurztraminer and Crémant d'Alsace amid monumental old casks.

pv.src: mappy POI (fr.mappy.com/poi/512ec73784aee927f3e3f076) + fr.wikipedia 'Cave historique des hospices de Strasbourg' (1 place de l'Hôpital) - coordinate stated in result text

places.ad: 6 Rue de la Gare, 67210 Obernai, France
places.w: The corridor's gastronomic summit — a two-MICHELIN-star table in Obernai where local terroir (foie gras, game, Alsace produce) is elegantly reinvented in a jewel-box dining room. Worth the short trip off the wine road from Strasbourg.

pv.src: mappy.fr venue POI (La Fourchette des Ducs, Obernai)

places.w: A genuinely Alsatian winstub behind one of Alsace's finest carved-timber Renaissance facades, built in 1605 by the bishopric's receiver Henri Katz. Warm wood, painted decor and the full canon — choucroute, pork cheeks braised in beer, chicken pot pie. A landmark stop at Saverne on the Nancy-Strasbourg corridor.

pv.src: mappy.fr venue POI (80 Grand'Rue, Saverne)

places.ad: 4 rue de Collonges au Mont d'Or, 68970 Illhaeusern, France
places.w: The grande dame of Alsace gastronomy on the banks of the Ill, in the Haeberlin family since 1882 and three-star from 1967 to 2018, now a two-MICHELIN-star Relais & Chateaux under Marc Haeberlin. Classic riverside dining: foie-gras terrine by the spoon, salmon souffle, the famous frog-leg mousseline.

pv.src: Etoiles d'Alsace / restaurant directory DMS 48d10'52.77"N 7d25'52.25"E; cross-checked to Illhaeusern (Wikipedia town 48.185,7.4356)

places.w: A MICHELIN-starred table set inside a genuine dismantled-and-rebuilt Alsatian half-timbered farmhouse in the Parc de l'Orangerie, where Eric Westermann cooks a season-driven, classically grounded cuisine. The signature frog-leg mousseline is a Strasbourg institution.

pv.src: Anchor: Parc de l'Orangerie (monument historique PA00085186, fr.wikipedia); venue sits inside park, ~park-scale precision

places.w: A two-MICHELIN-star destination in the 1920 villa René Lalique in the northern Vosges, with a Mario Botta-designed dining room and Paul Stradner's intelligent, delicate cuisine. Worth the drive for the crystal-and-cuisine setting.

pv.src: Wikidata Q97368012 (Villa Rene Lalique), DMS 48d55'07"N 7d21'52.672"E, Wingen-sur-Moder

places.ad: 30 rue du General de Gaulle, 67520 Marlenheim, France
places.w: A former posthouse at the gateway to the wine road, MICHELIN-starred since 1936 and run by the Husser family since 1930. Chef Michel Husser gives Alsace cooking a modern, refined turn around a picturesque paved courtyard.

pv.src: fr.wikipedia 'Le Cerf (restaurant)' / directory DMS 48d37'14"N 7d29'38"E; cross-checked to Marlenheim

places.w: One of Alsace's great biodynamic estates, run by the Faller women around the walled Clos des Capucins founded by Capuchin monks in 1612. Tastings of world-class Riesling, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer, including the Cuvee Colette and Sainte-Catherine bottlings.

pv.src: Directory POI (25 Route du Vin, Clos des Capucins); cross-checked to Kaysersberg

places.w: A rustic riverside bierstub-winstub tucked between the arms of the Ill by the Ponts Couverts for nearly fifty years, serving the full canon — choucroute royale, baeckeoffe, choucroute aux trois poissons. A classic Strasbourg tavern.

pv.src: Anchor: Ponts Couverts monument (fr.wikipedia / Monumentum PA00085192) 48d34'48.4"N 7d44'21.6"E; venue at 1 Ponts Couverts

places.w: A much-loved brasserie institution on Petite France's prettiest square, with a plane-shaded terrace over the Ill and a menu built on spatzle, salads, tarte flambee and pork knuckle. A reliable, atmospheric Petite France stop.

pv.src: Anchor: Place Benjamin-Zix / Petite France quarter (fr.wikipedia, en.wikipedia Petite France 48d34'51"N 7d44'26"E); venue on the square

places.w: Saarbrücken's two-MICHELIN-star flagship in the Nauwieser Viertel, in an 1890 Gründerzeit former school turned boutique hotel. Chef Silio Del Fabro — Gusto's Koch des Jahres 2026 — cooks supremely fresh, farm-sourced seasonal produce; the city's benchmark fine-dining table right in its creative quarter.

pv.src: Nauwieser Viertel (Wikidata Q1972159); Nauwieserstrasse 5

places.w: A century-old family restaurant-and-butcher in the village of Bliesen that has held a MICHELIN star for over two decades under Alexander and Anke Kunz. Precise French classics sit beside the house's own charcuterie and a famous Wiener Schnitzel — the Saarland's rural fine-dining destination and a Jeunes Restaurateurs member.

pv.src: Wikidata Q1535073 (St. Remigius, Bliesen); restaurant adjacent at Kirchstrasse 22

places.w: A tiny gastro-jewel in a Nauwieser-Viertel sandstone house (the birthplace of director Max Ophüls), run by ex-two-star chef Jens Jacob. Counter seats — 'le comptoir' — are the prize; evenings bring a modern four/five-course seasonal market menu. A MICHELIN-Guide selection.

pv.src: Saarbruecken St. Johann centre (St. Johanner Markt, Wikidata Q15848504); Foersterstrasse 15, town-level

places.w: The relaxed counterpart to Esplanade in the same boutique-hotel building, taking over the fine-dining rooms when the two-star is dark. Modern cooking in weekly-changing three- or four-course menus, one of them vegetarian — a MICHELIN-Guide address at an accessible price.

pv.src: Nauwieser Viertel (Wikidata Q1972159); Nauwieserstrasse 5

places.w: A French bistronomie address in a well-kept townhouse just outside the centre, carrying a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand for good-value cooking — confit chicken with scalloped potatoes, fjord trout with potato foam. Reopened in spring 2026 under new owners Josianne Lerner and Paul Stiel, with a lovely front terrace.

pv.src: Saarbruecken St. Johann (St. Johanner Markt, Wikidata Q15848504); Scheidter Strasse 66, town-level

places.w: A 25-year fixture on the St. Johanner Markt built entirely around the Saarland's potato canon — Hoorische, Gefillde, Geheirade and Dibbelabbes in a rustic room. The place to eat the region's home kitchen right in the old-town square.

pv.src: Wikidata Q15848504 (St. Johanner Markt); at no.32 on the square

places.w: Saarbrücken's beloved riverside beer garden on the Staden meadows beside the Saar — bratwurst off the grill, sandwiches and cool draught beer under the trees, with a playground next door. A relaxed local favourite for young and old alike.

pv.src: Saarbruecken St. Johann (St. Johanner Markt); Am Staden 13, town-level

places.w: One of the capital's oldest typical Luxembourgish tables, in the former Mousel brewery buildings in Clausen for some two centuries. Hearty local cooking — Judd mat Gaardebounen, choucroute garnie — washed down with the Clausel beer still brewed on the old brewery site.

pv.src: Clausen district (Wikidata Q519726); Montee de Clausen 46

places.w: A classic of the genre on the wooded edge of the Bambësch above Rollingergrund — a big hotel-restaurant with a huge terrace where Luxembourgish cooking is done simply but with care. A family standby for the national dish, name-checked by both ELLE and Paperjam.
